newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Arafat says nothing solid so far in Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says nothing solid so far in Mideast talks.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Wednesday tempered optimistic talk of a breakthrough in the stalled Middle East peace process and appealed to the European Union to help.

"Nothing was achieved yesterday," Arafat told a news conference the day after he met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy and they reopened the talks that had been in limbo since April over Israeli plans to build houses in Arab East Jerusalem.
"I am looking to achieve something concrete. We are not asking for the moon," Arafat said after meeting Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke.
"We are asking for what has been signed at the White House to be implemented completely and successfully," he added, referring to the "land for peace" agreement that launched the peace process.

Arafat's comments stood in stark contrast to confident remarks earlier by Levy after he met Manuel Marin, the European Commissioner with responsibility for relations with the Middle East and Development Aid.
"I am satisfied that things will change. We have entered a period of co-operation that I am sure will have good results," Levy told reporters.
The peace talks, first launched in Oslo in 1993, have been steadily sliding into crisis since March this year when Israelis began building 6,500 houses in Arab East Jerusalem.
Former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated in November 1995, and his successor Shimon Peres both stood by the accords.
Arafat and Rabin shared the Nobel peace prize in 1994 for their efforts for peace in the Middle East.
But current Prime Minister Benyamin Netanyahu, to international disapproval, gave the green light for the housing project.
"Mr Rabin, my partner, refused to carry on with the project. So did Peres," Arafat said. "It is very delicate."
On Tuesday Arafat and Levy, who have not met since April, appeared to be mutually optimistic about the chances for restarting the peace process.
However, Arafat said on Wednesday Levy had no mandate to discuss the thorny issue of East Jerusalem, and it was unclear what the position of the Israeli government would be.
"We are asking the European Union to help get results," he said. "It is very important that with their help we can save the peace process."
"We want something more concrete and more interventions from the European Union," Arafat added.
Tuesday's meeting between Arafat and Levy was brokered by the EU and took place on the fringes of a meeting in Brussels of EU foreign ministers.
On Wednesday both men said no timetable had been set for resuming full talks, although Levy said he was confident the two sides could get the agenda back on track.
